title: The bigger joy (290–295)
hookLine: if by leaving a small pleasure one finds a great one, the wise leave the small

lines: THE SMALL PLEASURE BLOCKS THE VIEW.
cards: There's a well-known experiment with children and marshmallows: one now, or two if you can wait. The same trade turns up at the dinner table, when the phone buzzes while the person across from you is mid-story.
Or the extra hour in bed, when the quiet morning walk was the plan. The small pleasure isn't evil. It just sits right in front of the bigger one, blocking the view.
A chapter the translator simply called miscellaneous opens with exactly this trade.

teach.b: Chapter twenty-one gathers verses that didn't fit elsewhere, and it starts with a plain one.

Verse two hundred ninety, in Max Müller's English: "If by leaving a small pleasure one sees a great pleasure, let a wise man leave the small pleasure, and look to the great." Notice the verse doesn't say pleasure is bad.
The Pali word is sukha: happiness, ease, sweetness. The verse wants more of it, not less. It's a trade, and the wise person makes the good one.

teach.h: A BAD TRADE: JOY BUILT ON PAIN.
teach.b: The next verse shows a bad trade: the one who seeks happiness for himself by causing pain to others gets tangled up in hatred and never gets free. Then the verses turn to attention.
People neglect what ought to be done and do what ought not, the text says, and their desires keep growing; but those who keep watch over the body, moment by moment, don't drift that way.
Then comes a startling pair, verses two hundred ninety-four and two hundred ninety-five.

teach.h: THE RIDDLE OF MOTHER, FATHER, KINGS.
teach.b: They say the true brahmana goes free, even after killing mother and father and two kings. Read on its own, it's shocking. The old commentary explains it as a riddle.

The mother is craving, the father is pride, the kings are two wrong views, and the kingdom is the senses and everything that rides on them. Kill those, and you walk free. It's yesterday's forest, told as a riddle.
The bigger joy, in the end, is the freedom on the far side of all the small trades.

how: Buddhist teachers often use verse 290 to explain renunciation not as loss but as trading a lesser happiness for a greater one; the riddle verses 294–295 are usually taught with the commentary's symbolic reading.

o: happiness, ease, a kind of sweetness
the suffering that comes from wanting
a selfish pleasure the wise must give up

games.q: match each piece of today's verses.

s: it says leave the small pleasure to find the great one: it wants more happiness, not less.
the verses about killing mother and father are read as a riddle
the old commentary reads the mother as craving, the father as pride, and the kings as wrong views.
chapter twenty-one has one single theme
Müller called it miscellaneous: it gathers verses on many themes.

games.q: it's dinner. your phone buzzes, and a friend across the table is mid-story. what would verse 290 weigh?
o: the buzz is small, the conversation is great: leave the small.
pleasure is dangerous, so enjoy neither.
check the phone; all pleasures are equal.
games.why: the verse asks for a trade: let the small pleasure go when it stands in front of a greater one.

practice: Bring to mind one small pleasure you reach for most days, a second coffee, one more episode, a few more minutes in bed, and ask what bigger joy it sometimes stands in front of: a conversation, a rested morning, a clear head.
You don't have to give anything up; just see the two side by side, the small and the great. Then let both go, and rest in the breath, which asks nothing of you.

wordCard.voice: Sukha. Happiness, ease: leave a small sukha when it hides a great one; the verse wants more happiness, not less.

orig.note: Pali sukha: happiness, ease; verse 290 speaks of small sukha and great sukha.

carryVoice: Your line: look to the great. Small joy and great joy are both sukha. Day two hundred twelve.

sources.work: The Dhammapada (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 10)
